title: Attack and defend: password guessing
blurb: Recognize brute-force and password-spraying attempts against SSH, and slow them down on the router.
purpose: Password guessing against SSH and VPN logins never stops on the Internet. In this lab you learn what a brute-force attack looks like in logs, and you slow it down with login protection while keeping your own admins able to log in.
scenario: R3's logs fill up overnight with failed SSH logins from addresses on the Internet. Work out which kind of password attack this is, then make R3 resist it without locking out the real admins.
topology:
Internet ── R3 (SSH on Gi0/0)
               admins from 10.10.99.0/24
objectives: Tell brute force, spraying and credential stuffing apart
Turn on login protection with an exception for the management network

steps.title: Three kinds of password attack
steps.learn: **Brute force** tries many passwords against one account. **Password spraying** tries one or two common passwords against many accounts, which stays under per-account lockout limits. **Credential stuffing** replays username and password pairs leaked from other sites.
steps.task: Match each pattern to the attack.

fields.label: 5,000 attempts at the account admin in an hour
Season2026! tried once against 400 different accounts
Email and password pairs from another site's breach tried in order

steps.title: Read the logs
steps.question:
R3 shows hundreds of lines like this, each from a different Internet address, all for the same user:

`%SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED: Login Failed [user: admin] [Source: 198.51.100.x] [localport: 22] [Reason: Login Authentication Failed]`

What is happening?

options.text: A distributed brute-force attack on the admin account, spread across many sources to avoid per-source blocking.

options.why: Spraying targets many accounts. Here every attempt is for admin.

options.text: A normal admin mistyping a password.
options.why: Hundreds of failures from many Internet addresses isn't human error.

steps.title: Slow it down
steps.learn: `login block-for` puts the router into **quiet mode** after too many failures, refusing all logins for a while. `login quiet-mode access-class` names an ACL of sources that may still log in during quiet mode, so the attack can't lock out your own team. `login on-failure log` records every failure.
steps.task: Create standard ACL **MGMT-OK** permitting **10.10.99.0/24**. Block logins for **300** seconds after **5** failures within **60** seconds, let **MGMT-OK** log in during quiet mode, and log failures.
steps.hint: `ip access-list standard MGMT-OK`, `permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255`, `login block-for 300 attempts 5 within 60`, `login quiet-mode access-class MGMT-OK`, `login on-failure log`.

commands.explain: Creates the ACL of sources that may still log in during an attack.
Blocks logins for 300 seconds after 5 failures within 60 seconds.

commands.note: Admins on 10.10.99.0/24 can still get in while the attack triggers quiet mode.
commands.explain: Lets the management subnet log in even while logins are blocked.

commands.output:
A login delay of 1 seconds is applied.
     Quiet-Mode access list MGMT-OK is applied.
     All failed login is logged.

     Router enabled to watch for login Attacks.
     If more than 5 login failures occur in 60 seconds or less,
       logins will be disabled for 300 seconds.

     Router presently in Quiet-Mode.
     Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 241 seconds.
     Restricted logins filtered by applied ACL MGMT-OK.
commands.note: The attack triggered quiet mode, and only the management network can log in.
commands.explain: Shows the login protection settings and whether quiet mode is active.

steps.title: The real fix
steps.question: Login protection slows guessing down. What removes the risk best?

options.text: Don't expose SSH to the Internet at all: allow it only from the management network or over the VPN, and use MFA or SSH keys for admins.

options.why: That cuts log noise, but scanners find other ports quickly. It's obscurity, not security.

options.text: Make the admin password longer and keep SSH open.
options.why: That helps, but the service is still exposed to every guesser on the Internet.

summary: Brute force, spraying and stuffing told apart, a distributed brute-force attack read from the logs, login quiet mode with a management exception and failure logging, and removing Internet exposure as the real fix.
